social_history.occupation: Retired professional soprano, now voice coach

neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented x4. Emotional about changes to her voice.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Tongue atrophy bilateral, visible fasciculations at rest. Dysarthria — nasal quality, hypophonic. Jaw jerk brisk. Palatal elevation asymmetric (right reduced).
neurological_exam.motor: Bilateral hand intrinsic weakness with wasting. Right shoulder abduction 4/5. Fasciculations visible in bilateral deltoids, triceps, and calves.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps 3+ bilaterally. Hoffmans bilateral. Bilateral Babinski positive.
neurological_exam.additional: Prominent bulbar-onset in professional singer — voice changes particularly distressing to this patient.

patient.chief_complaint: Progressive speech changes and bilateral hand weakness over 11 months
patient.history_present_illness: Mrs. V is a 64-year-old retired professional soprano and current voice coach who presents with an 11-month history of progressive dysarthria, voice changes, and bilateral hand weakness. As a professional voice user, she first noticed subtle changes in her vocal quality approximately 11 months ago, which she initially attributed to vocal fatigue or aging. Over the ensuing months, her speech became increasingly nasal and hypophonic, and she began to have difficulty sustaining high notes during her coaching sessions. She subsequently noticed progressive weakness in both hands, finding it increasingly difficult to demonstrate piano playing technique and to button her shirt. Approximately 6 months ago, her students began commenting on visible muscle twitching in her arms during lessons. Her husband noticed her tongue fasciculating approximately 4 months ago. She has no history of botulinum toxin injections to the vocal cords. Her levothyroxine dose has been stable for 3 years with consistent normal TSH. She has no dysphagia to solids but reports occasional coughing with thin liquids. She denies any cognitive changes. Her progression has been relentless and she reports marked functional decline over the past 6 months compared to her initial presentation.

findings.location: Bilateral corticospinal tracts — internal capsule, cerebral peduncles, and anterior brainstem
Bilateral cranial nerve XII nuclei (hypoglossal nuclei in dorsal medulla)

additional_observations: No mass effect on lower cranial nerves
mri.impression: 1. Bilateral symmetric T2/FLAIR hyperintensity of the corticospinal tracts from internal capsule to anterior brainstem. 2. Subtle bilateral T2 signal increase at the hypoglossal nuclei in the dorsal medulla. No brainstem structural lesion, no mass effect on lower cranial nerves, no white matter lesions. Exclusion studies.clinical_significance: Ordered to exclude an alternative cause; the result does not support one, which is what this case's diagnosis rests on

labs.interpretation: Rule-out studies do not confirm ALS. Targeted abnormalities are listed above.

findings.finding: Tongue: fibrillations +2, large polyphasic MUPs (chronic denervation/reinnervation), reduced recruitment. Mentalis: fasciculations. Consistent with bulbar lower motor neuron involvement.
Bilateral FDI, APB: fibrillations +2, positive sharp waves, large MUPs (duration >14ms). Bilateral deltoids: fasciculations +1. Cervical paraspinals C5-C7: fibrillations +1.
Bilateral tibialis anterior: fasciculations. Left gastrocnemius: fibrillations +1.
Median, ulnar, sural: normal amplitude and conduction velocities throughout. No sensory neuropathy.
Median motor (bilateral): CMAP amplitudes reduced (right 3.8 mV, left 3.2 mV; reference >4.5 mV). Normal distal latencies and conduction velocities. No conduction block.

quantitative_data.classification: Active and chronic denervation across body regions, meeting the electrodiagnostic criterion for widespread LMN involvement

specialized_test.impression: Active denervation and chronic reinnervation in bulbar, cervical, thoracic, and lumbosacral regions — four body regions involved. Normal sensory NCS throughout. Reduced CMAP amplitudes bilaterally; normal distal latencies and conduction velocities; no conduction block. Findings indicate a widespread disorder of lower anterior horn cells

body_imaging.impression: Cervical and thoracic cord imaged; no compressive lesion and no cord signal change to explain the deficit.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), bulbar-onset with early respiratory involvement

differential.key_features: Bulbar predominance; EMG confirms spinal involvement (bulbar-onset ALS)

tool_parameters.query: ALS diagnostic criteria Awaji Gold Coast AAN practice parameter

optimal_actions.action: Check interactions before initiating riluzole 50 mg twice daily; review baseline LFTs and CBC and counsel on monitoring
optimal_actions.expected_finding: No major interactions for typical chronic medications; advise alcohol and grapefruit-juice avoidance (CYP1A2 modulators); monthly LFTs for first 3 months

optimal_actions.action: Obtain brain MRI to exclude structural, brainstem, inflammatory, demyelinating or neoplastic ALS mimics
optimal_actions.expected_finding: No better structural explanation for progressive upper and lower motor-neuron findings

optimal_actions.action: Obtain cervical and thoracic spinal-cord MRI to exclude compressive myelopathy and other cord lesions
optimal_actions.expected_finding: No compressive, neoplastic, inflammatory or demyelinating cord mimic

optimal_actions.action: Order a baseline treatable-mimic panel, adding only phenotype-specific infectious, immune, paraprotein or metabolic tests
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Exclude common hematologic, renal/hepatic, electrolyte, calcium, thyroid, B12/folate, muscle and inflammatory alternatives; tests do not confirm ALS

optimal_actions.action: Perform EMG/NCS across bulbar, cervical, thoracic and lumbosacral regions using ALS electrodiagnostic criteria
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Active and chronic neurogenic change in multiple regions with preserved sensory studies and no conduction block

optimal_actions.action: Obtain baseline FVC/VC and SNIP or MIP after suspected ALS is established; this is a safety and management assessment, not a diagnostic confirmation
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Quantify respiratory involvement and need for surveillance or non-invasive ventilation

optimal_actions.action: Offer an ALS gene panel including C9orf72 and SOD1 after pre-test counselling; do not embed genetics in a routine blood panel
optimal_actions.expected_finding: A pathogenic result can affect counselling, family risk and gene-targeted therapy/trial eligibility; a negative result does not exclude ALS

useless_tools.rationale: ALS is a motor-neuron disease without cortical electrical signature; EEG has no diagnostic role and adds cost without benefit.
ECG is unrelated to motor neuron disease and not part of the standard ALS workup absent specific cardiac symptoms or pre-medication QTc checks.
Echocardiography is unrelated to ALS diagnosis; no indication absent comorbid cardiac disease.
Cardiac monitoring has no role in ALS diagnostic workup.
MRI is the standard structural study for ALS workup; head CT adds no diagnostic value and exposes the patient to ionizing radiation.
Amyloid PET has no role in ALS diagnosis (motor-neuron rather than amyloid pathology) and carries a high cost.
DaTscan evaluates nigrostriatal dopaminergic integrity; it has no role in ALS, which spares the dopaminergic system.
FDG-PET has no established diagnostic role in ALS and adds substantial cost.

critical_actions: Perform EMG/NCS sampling the bulbar region plus ≥2 spinal regions to document lower-motor-neuron involvement and exclude conduction block.
Obtain brain MRI to exclude structural mimics (cervical myelopathy, demyelinating disease, brainstem tumor).
Order a mimic-exclusion lab panel (CK, B12, TSH, HIV, RPR, SPEP, anti-GM1 IgM, androgen receptor CAG repeat in males).
Measure baseline respiratory function (FVC, MIP/MEP, SNIP) to inform NIV timing.
Obtain a swallowing evaluation by speech-language pathology given dysphagia and aspiration risk.
Apply Awaji-Shima 2008 / Gold Coast 2020 criteria to confirm the diagnosis.
Initiate riluzole 50 mg twice daily after baseline LFTs unless contraindicated; arrange monthly LFT monitoring for the first 3 months.
Refer to a multidisciplinary ALS clinic for SLP, dietetics, respiratory, and social-work input.
contraindicated_actions: Do not commit the patient to cervical spine surgery on the basis of incidental spondylotic changes when EMG findings extend beyond the cervical cord.
Do not start chronic immunosuppression (steroids, IVIG, plasma exchange) for ALS — there is no benefit and treatment delays correct diagnosis.
Do not defer respiratory assessment in a symptomatic patient — even mild FVC reduction warrants close monitoring and NIV planning.
Do not dismiss bulbar or progressive symptoms as functional / psychiatric without a complete neurological workup.
Do not continue oral feeding without a swallowing assessment given documented dysphagia and aspiration risk.
key_reasoning_points: Diagnosis requires evidence of both upper-motor-neuron involvement (hyperreflexia, Babinski, Hoffman, brisk jaw jerk, spasticity) and lower-motor-neuron involvement (atrophy, fasciculations, EMG denervation) with progressive spread, while excluding mimics — Awaji 2008 / Gold Coast 2020.

EMG in bulbar plus ≥2 spinal regions documenting fibrillations, positive sharp waves, complex fasciculation potentials, and large-amplitude long-duration polyphasic MUPs with reduced recruitment satisfies the electrodiagnostic criterion.
Normal sensory NCS and absence of conduction block are pivotal: they exclude common mimics including multifocal motor neuropathy, CIDP, and Kennedy disease.
Mild-to-moderate CK elevation (2–5× ULN) is consistent with ALS and does not itself indicate a primary myopathy.
Cervical spondylotic changes on MRI are common incidental findings in the at-risk age group; bulbar findings or multi-region EMG denervation cannot be attributed to cervical disease.
Baseline FVC, MIP/MEP, and SNIP/NIF inform NIV timing — NIV initiation at FVC <50% predicted or SNIP <40 cmH₂O prolongs survival and improves quality of life.
Bulbar-onset disease carries a worse prognosis; early NIV planning and swallowing/feeding strategy are higher priority than in limb-onset disease.

July 2026 review applied end to end: EMG/NCS is the required ALS-specific test; brain and cord MRI and targeted labs exclude mimics; respiratory function is a recommended safety baseline; genetics is separately offered after counselling; CSF is absent except in five atypical mimic work-ups.
